criterion_notes.c1: Examines municipal potable water supply and sewage service coverage in Rio Branco, Acre, Brazil, using SNIS attendance indicators (IN055, IN023, IN056, IN024) for 2018–2019.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and, on close inspection, an exposure-grounded plain reading. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, no rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access) is empirically examined. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses regulatory concepts—AGEAC's first-cycle ACERTAR data-certification audit, the Sunshine regulation model, and background narrative on Law 14.026/2020 and historical institutional reorganizations (DOV, SAAE, SANACRE, DEPASA, SAERB)—but Sunshine regulation is used solely by the authors as an ex-post benchmarking rubric to grade 2018–2019 SNIS indicators into Ideal/Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory intervals, ACERTAR audited operational equipment calibration and SNIS reporting accuracy rather than access governance, and statutory/institutional references are unanalysed macro-governance background (Law 14.026/2020 postdates the 2018–2019 data).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical descriptive analysis of secondary administrative data from SNIS and AGEAC's Inspection Report and first-cycle ACERTAR Certification Report for DEPASA covering 2018–2019.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal water and sewage service access/coverage outcomes: total water coverage (IN055 = 53.16%), urban water coverage (IN023 = 57.19%), total sewage coverage (IN056 = 20.49% in 2018; 21.65% in 2019) and urban sewage coverage (IN024 = 22.25% in 2018; 23.52% in 2019), classified into Ideal/Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory tiers alongside efficiency and water-quality indicators.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (Municipality of Rio Branco / state utility DEPASA in 2018–2019), outcomes (SNIS coverage, efficiency and quality indicators) and descriptive benchmarking design are identifiable, but an empirical governance/legal exposure affecting service access cannot be identified because the Sunshine regulation model is the authors' analytical classification rubric rather than an evaluated exposure.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Portuguese (with Portuguese, English and Spanish abstracts), which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

evidence_quotes.quote: avaliar o desempenho e a vulnerabilidade dos serviços de água e esgoto no município de Rio Branco, Acre, no período de 2018 a 2019, aplicados ao modelo Sunshine.

A construção da base de dados sobre o Saneamento Básico foi obtida por meio de solicitação formal de informações junto à Divisão técnica de Saneamento Básico da Agência Reguladora dos Serviços Públicos do estado do Acre

Utilizada para regular o comportamento das operadoras dos serviços de água e esgoto, a abordagem metodológica escolhida foi a denominada Sunshine, na qual cada indicador selecionado é avaliado com base nos intervalos recomendados pelo Plano Nacional de Saneamento Básico (PLANSAB)

De forma geral, identificou-se que o prestador possui procedimentos em desacordo com o Plano Nacional de Saneamento Básico, o que pode ser visto em sua dimensão operacional na qual o prestador apresenta, em sua maioria, falhas na precisão dos equipamentos e falta de procedimentos operacionais.
Com relação à população urbana atendida (IN023) o município apresentou 57,19% de cobertura. Com relação à cobertura total, 53,16% da população total é atendida

Apesar deste ter apresentado um aumento, passando de 20,49% para 21,65% entre os anos 2018 e 2019, respectivamente, a prestação do serviço quanto ao atendimento total de esgoto no município ainda se configura como insatisfatório.

raw_response.exposure: No empirical legal/governance exposure affecting access (Sunshine regulation is applied by the authors as an analytical benchmarking rubric to classify 2018–2019 SNIS indicators; AGEAC's ACERTAR audit assessed utility equipment/SNIS data reliability; statutory and institutional history are unanalysed background)
raw_response.outcome: Municipal water supply coverage (IN055 total water coverage: 53.16%; IN023 urban water coverage: 57.19%) and sewage collection coverage (IN056 total sewage coverage: 20.49% in 2018 and 21.65% in 2019; IN024 urban sewage coverage: 22.25% in 2018 and 23.52% in 2019), plus SNIS operational efficiency and water-quality compliance tiers
raw_response.population_and_sample: Municipality of Rio Branco, Acre, Brazil (estimated population 419,452: 385,895 urban and 33,556 rural); unit of analysis is the municipal water and sewage system operated by state utility DEPASA in 2018–2019
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E03: Wrong exposure). Although this Portuguese full-text study empirically reports 2018–2019 municipal water supply and sewage coverage indicators for Rio Branco, Acre (from SNIS and AGEAC's first-cycle ACERTAR audit of DEPASA), it does not examine any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing service access. Instead, the authors use the 'Sunshine regulation' model purely as an ex-post benchmarking rubric to classify 17 technical, water-quality, and coverage SNIS indicators into Ideal, Satisfactory, and Unsatisfactory intervals against PLANSAB and Portaria MS 05/2017 reference thresholds, while ACERTAR audit observations address operational equipment calibration and data-reporting reliability, and discussions of Law 14.026/2020 and historical utility reorganizations serve only as unanalysed background. Because no governance exposure governing access is empirically evaluated, the study fails Criterion 2 and Criterion 5 under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and an exposure-grounded plain reading.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive empirical case study / regulatory performance indicator benchmarking (secondary SNIS and AGEAC ACERTAR audit data, 2018–2019)
